newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam acknowledges its President's illness.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam acknowledges its President's illness.

text.p: Vietnam ackowledged to its people for the first time on Thursday that a member of the country's powerful leadership triumvirate, President Le Duc Anh, was ill.

The news was carried by most official dailies and on state television by way of explanation for Anh's absence from a formal welcoming ceremony on Wednesday for South Korea's visiting President Kim Young-sam.
Kim was met instead by Communist Party chief Do Muoi, who briefly discussed the issue in response to a question from Kim.
"President Le Duc Anh, who couldn't attend because of illness, sent his greetings to the Korean President," the English-language daily Vietnam News said in its only comment.
The public acknowledgement came almost a week after the 75-year-old general was admitted to Hanoi's 108 Army hospital suffering blood pressure problems.
The few medical details that have emerged have indicated Anh suffered a stroke. Political sources said he was paralysed down one side of his body and would not be returning to work.
"The doctors say his survival is sure," said one Vietnamese analyst. "But his staying out of work is also sure."
Few further details of Anh's situation were available on Thursday, but there was a growing consensus among foreign diplomats that Anh's health would mean his being replaced.
"There has been no announcement yet of duties being transferred to Madame Binh," one said. "We'll wait for a while to see, but we're expecting Madame Binh will be (acting) president for a while."
Madame Nguyen Thi Binh is the vice-president, which is a figurehead rather than executive political role.
Under Vietnam's constitution, the appointment of any new president must be approved by the National Assembly.
The assembly has just ended its autumn session and, barring an emergency meeting, is not expected to meet again before March of next year.
But analysts say replacing Anh would be difficult as he occupies a key position of influence over the military and security apparatus.
The other members of the leadership -- representing a balance of power interests -- are the reformist Prime Minister Vo Van Kiet, 73, and Communist Party Secretary General Do Muoi, 79.
All three were expected to be replaced earlier this year at a major Communist Party congress. But the party opted instead for an extension of their terms in office.
